A.explanation: This is the original power before the change, $P = (0.20)^2 \times 12 = 0.48 \text{ W}$, not the power after doubling the current.

B.explanation: This doubles the original $0.48 \text{ W}$ to $0.96 \text{ W}$, but power in a fixed resistor is proportional to $I^2$, not to $I$.

C.explanation: With new current $0.40 \text{ A}$, $P = I^2R = (0.40)^2 \times 12 = 1.92 \text{ W} \approx 1.9 \text{ W}$.

D.explanation: This is much larger than $I^2R$ with $0.40 \text{ A}$ and $12 \text{ } \Omega$ gives; substitution gives about $1.9 \text{ W}$.

hints: Notice the resistance stays fixed at $12 \text{ } \Omega$ while the current changes from $0.20 \text{ A}$ to $0.40 \text{ A}$ when doubled.
Recall for a resistor that power depends on current squared, $P = I^2R$, so doubling $I$ multiplies $P$ by four.
First work out the original $0.48 \text{ W}$, then multiply by four or directly evaluate $(0.40)^2 \times 12$.
walkthrough: Identify the fixed quantity and the change: $R = 12 \text{ } \Omega$ is constant, initial $I_1 = 0.20 \text{ A}$, new $I_2 = 2 \times 0.20 = 0.40 \text{ A}$.
State the governing rule for heating in a resistor: $P = I^2R$. Because $R$ is constant, $P$ is proportional to $I^2$.
Calculate the original power to check the scale: $P_1 = (0.20)^2 \times 12 = 0.040 \times 12 = 0.48 \text{ W}$.
Calculate the new power with the new current: $P_2 = (0.40)^2 \times 12 = 0.16 \times 12 = 1.92 \text{ W}$.
Check units and precision: power is in $\text{W}$, and $1.92 \text{ W}$ rounds to $1.9 \text{ W}$ with two significant figures. This is option C.
